title: Producers I: keys, partitions and ordering
goal: By the end, you can explain how a producer picks a partition for each record, work out by hand which partition a key lands in, say exactly which order is kept and which isn't, and choose a key and a partition count for a topic of payments.
opening:
Picture paying for a coffee, then asking for a refund a minute later because the order was wrong. That evening your bank's app lists the refund first, and for a moment your balance looks as if the café paid you. In a program that keeps account balances, it's worse: a refund for a payment it has never seen.

It's easy to assume that order can't break. Kafka, a program that keeps logs of messages and lets other programs read them, stores each record in a log, and a log keeps its order. That's true, and it's why smart people stop there. A topic, though, is several logs side by side.

The cluster: KRaft, replicas and the ISR made each of those logs safe on three computers. It left one question for the program that writes: which log gets each payment? In this lesson, we'll work out the rule a producer uses, send a thousand payments to see which order survives, and grow a topic to watch the rule shift. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A topic of payments is split into 6 partitions, separate logs that 6 consumers read side by side, one partition each. A program sends a payment and then its refund for account `acct-42`, one after the other, and labels both with the account number as their key. Which is true?
options: The refund can be handled first, because six consumers work in parallel
Both go to the same partition, so the one consumer that reads it sees the payment first
Kafka orders every record in the topic by its time, so the order is safe
Order is kept only if the program picks the partition number for each record itself
warmup.why: The key decides the partition: the producer turns it into a number, and the same key always gives the same number. A partition is a log, read in order, and each one has a single reader among the 6. Six consumers in parallel is the tempting answer, but each account's records still have only one reader. Kafka keeps no order across partitions, by time or otherwise. And there's no need to pick partitions by hand: the key already pins the account to one.

sections.h: Which partition gets the payment: the key and the hash
sections.body:
The coffee-shop payments app sends every card payment and every refund to Kafka. Each one travels as a record: a key, a value (the payment itself) and a few extra fields. The `payments` topic, Kafka's name for one stream of records, is split into 6 partitions. Each partition is a separate log, numbered 0 to 5. A log only ever adds records at its end, and numbers each one with the next offset. Splitting lets several computers and several readers share the work, as Partitions and segments on disk explained.

When the app calls `send()`, one of the six has to get the record. The broker, the Kafka server that stores partitions, doesn't choose. The producer does: the part of the Kafka library that sends records, running inside the app, before the record leaves the app's computer. Then it sends the record to that partition's leader, the broker that holds the partition's main copy.

What should the rule be? The simplest one is round robin, taking turns: record 1 to partition 0, record 2 to partition 1, and so on. It spreads the load perfectly, and it breaks payments at once. The payment for `acct-42` lands in partition 0 and its refund in partition 1. Two consumers read those partitions, each at its own pace, so the refund can be handled first. The program that keeps balances then sees a refund for a payment it has never heard of. It rejects it, or worse, books it wrong.

So the rule needs one property: every record of one account goes to the same partition. Then that account's records sit in one log, in the order they were added, and a log keeps its order. The rule must also work without the producers talking to each other. A busy app runs as several copies of the same program on several computers, and none of them asks the others where a record went.

A post room solves the same problem with pigeonholes, the rows of small open boxes where letters wait to be collected. Every clerk who drops off a letter works out the box from the account number on the envelope, using the same sum. Letters for one account end up in one box, stacked in the order they came, and no clerk needs to ask another. In Kafka's terms, the account number is the record's key, the box is the partition, and the sum is a hash.

A **hash function** turns any bytes into a number. The same bytes always give the same number, and bytes that differ by one character give numbers that look unrelated, so keys spread out evenly. The record's **key** is the input. It's optional, and Kafka itself gives it no meaning: you choose it. For payments, the account id is the usual choice.

The default partitioner, the code in the Java client library that picks the partition, takes four steps:

1. Turn the key into bytes. `StringSerializer` turns `"acct-17"` into its 7 bytes of UTF-8, the usual way to store text as bytes.
2. Hash the bytes with murmur2, a fast hash function that gives a 32-bit number, the size of a Java `int`. For `acct-17` it gives -1871546916.
3. Clear the sign bit (`hash & 0x7fffffff`). A Java `int` can be negative, and its leftmost bit, the sign bit, says whether it is. A partition number can't be negative, so the producer keeps the other 31 bits. -1871546916 becomes 275936732.
4. Take the remainder after dividing by the number of partitions: 275936732 % 6 = 2.

So `acct-17` goes to partition 2 of 6, from every producer, every time. Notice step 3: it isn't `Math.abs`, the usual way to make a number positive. `Math.abs(-1871546916) % 6` is 0, so a test or a tool that predicts partitions with `Math.abs` gets most keys with a negative hash wrong. The demo in The cluster: KRaft, replicas and the ISR put `acct-17` in partition 2 of 3, and now you can check why: 275936732 % 3 is 2.

The rule lives in each client library, not in Kafka. A client library is the code a program uses to talk to Kafka, and each language has its own. Programs written in Python, Go or C# often use librdkafka, a library written in C, which hashes keys with a different function, CRC32, by default. So a Go program and a Java program writing the same key can pick different partitions, unless the Go program sets `partitioner=murmur2_random`. The post room fails the same way: a clerk who uses a different sum puts letters in the wrong box.

Two ways skip the hash entirely. A record built with an explicit partition number goes to that partition, and the setting `partitioner.class` plugs in a rule of your own. Next, we'll see exactly which order the key protects, and which it can't.

aside.title: Why doesn't the broker pick the partition?
aside.body: Because there's no single broker to ask. Each partition has its own leader, often on a different computer, and the producer must know which one to send to before it sends anything. Asking one central place for every record would add a round trip, a message there and an answer back, to every payment. That place would also become the bottleneck for the whole topic. Working it out locally takes well under a microsecond and needs nobody's permission, and its price is the last point of this section: every producer must use the same rule.

try.title: Hash a key by hand, then let the producer do it
steps: From the `labs` folder, start a one-broker Kafka: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml up -d --wait` (Docker runs it in a container, a sealed-off box on your computer). Then create a topic with 6 partitions: `docker compose -f env/kafka.yml exec kafka /opt/kafka/bin/kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server localhost:9092 --create --topic accounts --partitions 6`.

Run the demo (command below). For four keys it prints the murmur2 hash, the hash with its sign bit cleared, the remainder after dividing by the partition count, and the partition the real producer chose.
`acct-18` differs from `acct-17` in one character. Predict: will its hash be close? Then run the demo again with `-Pargs=acct-18` added.
Keep the broker running for the next Try its.

code.title: PartitionForDemo.java

alt.title: PartitionForDemo.kt
alt.src:
package sfz.msg.l05.demo

import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.KafkaProducer
import org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.ProducerRecord
import org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
import org.apache.kafka.common.utils.Utils

/**
 * For each key: the murmur2 hash, the hash made positive, the partition that arithmetic gives,
 * and the partition the real producer chose when it sent a record with that key to the topic "accounts".
 */
fun main(args: Array<String>) {
    val keys = args.toList().ifEmpty { listOf("acct-17", "acct-42", "acct-99", "card-1") }
    val config = mapOf<String, Any>(
        "bootstrap.servers" to "localhost:9092", // env/kafka.yml
        "key.serializer" to StringSerializer::class.java,
        "value.serializer" to StringSerializer::class.java,
    )
    KafkaProducer<String, String>(config).use { producer ->
        val n = producer.partitionsFor("accounts").size
        println("topic accounts has $n partitions")
        println("%-9s %12s %11s %5s   %s".format("key", "murmur2", "positive", "% $n", "producer chose"))
        for (key in keys) {
            val hash = Utils.murmur2(key.toByteArray(Charsets.UTF_8)) // the bytes StringSerializer sends
            val positive = Utils.toPositive(hash)                     // hash and 0x7fffffff
            val chosen = producer.send(ProducerRecord("accounts", key, "auth 10.00 EUR")).get().partition()
            println("%-9s %12d %11d %5d   partition %d".format(key, hash, positive, positive % n, chosen))
        }
    }
}

try.expect:
```text
topic accounts has 6 partitions
key            murmur2    positive   % 6   producer chose
acct-17    -1871546916   275936732     2   partition 2
acct-42    -1294421753   853061895     3   partition 3
acct-99    -1758549442   388934206     4   partition 4
card-1       830907359   830907359     5   partition 5
```
The remainder and the producer's choice agree on every line, and you'll get the same numbers, because the hash depends only on the key's bytes. Three of the four hashes are negative. Clearing the sign bit turns -1871546916 into 275936732, which is 2^31 minus 1871546916, not its absolute value. `acct-18` hashes to 212957696, nothing like its neighbour, and still lands in partition 2. With 6 partitions, any two keys share one about one time in six. (The Kotlin demo prints the same table.)

refs.title: Confluent: the importance of standardized hashing across producers

sections.h: Order per key, and none across the topic
sections.body:
Records with the same key go to the same partition, and a partition only adds at its end. So if one producer sends the payment for `acct-42` before its refund, the leader appends them in that order, and every consumer of that partition reads them in that order. That's the whole ordering promise: **order within one partition, so order per key**.

It's also what a plain queue can't give when several workers share it: two messages about one account can go to two workers and finish in either order. Queues and brokers: acknowledgements, redelivery and fan-out met that problem. In Kafka, consumers that share the reading of a topic form a consumer group, and within a group each partition has one reader at a time. So one account's records are never being handled by two consumers at once.

Across partitions there's no order at all. Partition 0 and partition 3 are two logs, maybe on two brokers, and nothing records that a record in one was sent before a record in the other. A consumer that reads several partitions gets them in whatever order its requests come back: a run from partition 3, then a run from partition 0. In the post room, nobody can say whether a letter in box 2 came before one in box 5, and nobody needs to. The stepper below shows it with six payments.

Can you get one order for the whole topic? Only with one partition. Partitions and segments on disk put a number on that: one partition means one consumer per group, about 500 payments a second if each takes 2 ms. Almost no payment system needs one order for everything. What it needs is order per account, and a key gives you that while the load spreads over every partition.

The promise has two limits. First, it's the order in which records reach the leader. Two copies of your program that send records for the same account at the same moment race each other, and the leader appends whichever arrives first. If the real-world order matters, let one copy of the program own each account, or put a version number in each record for the consumer to check. Second, the producer's own retries, its automatic second attempts after an error, can swap records inside one producer. Producers II: batching, acks and idempotence shows how, and the setting, on by default, that prevents it.

The Try it below sends 1,000 payments for 10 accounts into the 6 partitions of `accounts`, then reads them back. Look at how the 10 keys spread. Partition 4 gets three accounts and partition 1 gets one. With 10 keys, hashing is lumpy; with 100,000 accounts, each partition gets close to a sixth.

Every record with a key now has its place. Next, we'll see what the producer does with records that have no key at all.

stepper.intro: Six payments, three accounts, three partitions. Watch which order survives.

Every account uses exactly one partition, and every account's 100 records came back in send order. The stream as a whole broke at the 100th record. The consumer handed out all of partition 2 first (`acct-1`, seq 0 to 990), then moved to partition 3, which starts with seq 5. Which partition comes first can differ on your run; the per-key lines won't. Partition 4 holds three accounts and partition 1 holds one: 10 keys spread unevenly.

sections.h: Records with no key go in sticky runs
sections.body:
Some records have no key: a note that someone logged in, a measurement taken every second, a line from a program's own log. Any partition will do, so the producer is free to pick. What it picks decides how well the records travel together.

A **batch** is a group of records for the same partition that travels to the broker in one request. The producer collects records per partition and sends each batch as a unit. Producers II: batching, acks and idempotence opens up how. Here we only need the effect. A request carrying 100 records costs about as much as a request carrying one, so full batches are cheap and nearly empty ones are waste. The post room sends letters in bags, one bag per box, and a bag with one letter in it still needs a trip.

Before Kafka 2.4, a record without a key went to the next partition in turn, round robin. That spread perfectly and batched badly. With 6 partitions, records in a row went to six different batches, so each batch filled six times more slowly, and many requests carried one or two records.

Kafka 2.4 made the producer sticky: it kept sending to one partition until that partition's batch was full or sent, then picked another. (The change came from KIP-480. A KIP, a Kafka Improvement Proposal, is one of the numbered documents in which Kafka's developers propose a change.) Batches got bigger, but a new problem showed up. A slow broker sends its batches later, so its partitions stayed the current choice for longer and collected more records, which made the broker slower still. In the test behind KIP-794, one broker received about 46.8 MB while each of the other two got about 9 MB.

Kafka 3.3 (KIP-794) fixed the rule. The producer now switches partitions after a fixed amount of data: between `batch.size` bytes (16 KB by default) and twice that, at the end of a batch when it can. It picks the next partition at random, but leans away from partitions with long queues, so a slow broker gets less new data instead of more. That leaning is `partitioner.adaptive.partitioning.enable`, on by default. With `partitioner.availability.timeout.ms` (0 by default, which means off), the producer can also skip a partition whose broker stops answering.

None of this applies to records with a key. A keyed record goes to its hash partition even when that partition's leader is down. It waits, retries and, if the leader stays away, fails with a timeout. Kafka won't move an account's payment to another partition to save time, because that would break the account's order. If you do want keyed records spread like unkeyed ones, `partitioner.ignore.keys=true` does it. The key is still stored with each record, and per-key order is gone.

So the key decides where each payment goes. Next, we'll choose the key itself, and see why the number of partitions has to stay put once we have.

try.title: No keys, then keys ignored
steps: Run the demo with no keys: add `-Pargs=no-keys` to the command (the command below already has it). Read the `in send order:` line: how many records in a row went to one partition?
Run it once more with `-Pargs=ignore-keys`. The records have keys again, but the producer is told to ignore them. Predict the per-key lines first.

code.title: KeyOrderDemo.java

alt.title: KeyOrderDemo.kt

try.expect:
With `no-keys`:
```text
mode no-keys: 1000 records to accounts (6 partitions)
in send order: p3 x349, p5 x651 (2 runs)
whole stream: in send order
```
With `ignore-keys` (account lines trimmed):
```text
mode ignore-keys: 1000 records to accounts (6 partitions)
in send order: p5 x327, p3 x271, p4 x402 (3 runs)
  acct-1   partitions [3, 4, 5]      in send order: no
  ...
  acct-10  partitions [3, 4, 5]      in send order: no
whole stream: out of send order at read #673 (seq 0 came right after seq 999)
```
The producer stayed on one partition for about 350 records, about 32 KB: twice `batch.size`. It may switch after 16 KB only if that partition's open batch is exactly full at that moment, which rarely lines up, so it usually runs on to the cap of twice `batch.size`. A run can look longer than the cap: the next partition is picked at random, nothing stops the pick from landing on the same partition again, and then two runs sit back to back. Your partitions and run lengths will differ for the same reason. The `no-keys` whole-stream line can go either way, depending on which partition the consumer reads first. With `ignore-keys`, every account is spread over three partitions, and none of them comes back in order.

sections.h: Choosing the key, and keeping the partition count fixed
sections.body:
The key decides two things at once: what stays in order, and how evenly the work spreads. So pick it for the order you need, then check the spread.

For payments, the account id is usually right. Every change to one balance stays in order, and a large bank has hundreds of thousands of accounts, so the partitions fill evenly. The payment id spreads even better, and keeps one payment's own records together, such as the payment and its refund. But then two payments on one account can be handled in either order.

The shop id looks natural for a topic that feeds the nightly payouts, the money the company pays each shop for its day's sales. (The labs call shops merchants, so this key would be a merchant id.) It's often a trap. If one big shop brings 30% of all payments, its partition gets 30% of the records. The one consumer that reads that partition then does several times the work of the others. Adding consumers doesn't help, because a partition has one reader per group. A key that piles traffic onto one partition like this is a **hot key**, the problem the Partitioning track met in Partitioning: consistent hashing and hot keys.

The other half of the rule is the number of partitions. The hash never changes, but the remainder depends on the number you divide by. Grow `accounts` from 6 to 8 partitions, and `acct-1` moves from partition 2 to partition 6. Most keys move. A key stays put only if its hash leaves the same remainder for 6 and for 8. That holds for 6 of every 24 hash values (24 is the smallest number that both 6 and 8 divide into), so about three keys in four change partition. The lab checks that number on 10,000 keys. Consistent hashing, a way of hashing in which adding a box moves only a few keys, was the Partitioning track's fix for this in databases. Kafka's producer still uses the plain remainder, so the partition count of a keyed topic is, in practice, fixed.

A key that moves breaks its own order. Records of `acct-1` written before the change are in partition 2, and newer ones go to partition 6. If partition 6's consumer is caught up while partition 2's is still behind, the new records are handled before the old ones. A running producer also keeps the old partition count until it refreshes its view of the cluster (`metadata.max.age.ms`, 5 minutes by default). For a while, two producers can put one key in two places. The consumer documentation warns of one more trap. A consumer set to start from the newest records (`auto.offset.reset=latest`) can silently skip records written to the new partitions before it notices them.

The usual reason to grow a topic is that consumers have fallen behind, and more partitions allow more consumers. The command succeeds, nothing logs a warning, and the speed does improve. That's why the broken order surprises people.

**The partition count is part of every key's address. Choose it once.**

So decide the count up front, with room for a few years of growth; Share groups and running Kafka in production covers sizing. If you must grow a keyed topic, stop the producers, let the consumers finish, add the partitions, then restart. Or create a new topic with more partitions and move to it. The post room breaks the same way: add two boxes, and the sum sends most accounts to a new box, while their old letters stay in the old one.

That's where today's rule stops. It decides where a record goes, but not when it leaves the producer, or whether it arrives.

Before, with 6 partitions, the ten accounts were in partitions 2, 5, 5, 4, 0, 3, 4, 1, 0, 4. After (trimmed to the first and last lines):
```text
topic accounts has 8 partitions
key            murmur2    positive   % 8   producer chose
acct-1       294059390   294059390     6   partition 6
acct-2      2084802707  2084802707     3   partition 3
...
acct-10      981674020   981674020     4   partition 4
```

The hashes didn't change; only the number we divide by did. Five of the ten moved (`acct-1`, `acct-2`, `acct-3`, `acct-6`, `acct-9`) and five stayed (`acct-4`, `acct-5`, `acct-7`, `acct-8`, `acct-10`). Over many keys about three in four move; ten keys is a small sample. Every record those five accounts wrote before the change is still in its old partition.

java.title: Java

kotlin.title: Kotlin

compare.note: The key is the second argument in both; leave it out (or pass null), and the record goes in a sticky run instead. The second argument to `send` is a callback, a function the producer calls once the broker has answered. Kotlin passes it as a trailing lambda, a function written after the call's parentheses, which works because `Callback` is a Java interface with one method. The callback runs on the producer's own network thread, so keep it short: log or count, and never wait for anything inside it. Both versions work out the generic types from the arguments, and both hash `payment.accountId` with murmur2 when the record is sent.

worked.title: Measure how evenly a key spreads before you choose it

steps.say: The team that pays the shops each night wants a topic called `settlements` (after the trade's word for paying the shops), keyed by shop id, on 12 partitions. The code calls a shop a merchant. Before agreeing, take a sample of a day's keys, here a list of 100,000 merchant ids, one per payment, and count where the default partitioner would put each one. `Utils` is `org.apache.kafka.common.utils.Utils`, the class that holds Kafka's own murmur2.

Turn the counts into one number: the busiest partition divided by the average. 1.0 is a perfect spread. The busiest partition's consumer sets the pace for the whole group, so this ratio is roughly how much slower the group runs than it would with a perfect spread.
steps.alt_code:
// 2. skew = busiest partition / average partition
val average = sampleMerchantIds.size / 12.0
val busiest = perPartition.max()
println("skew %.2f".format(busiest / average))

steps.say: Read the numbers. If one shop has 30% of the payments, its partition alone holds 30,000 of 100,000 records, against an average of about 8,333. So the skew is at least 3.6: one consumer does 3.6 times the average work, and adding consumers changes nothing. Run the same count on account ids and you get close to 1.0, because no single account is a large share.

So key `settlements` by account id (or by payment id, if the payouts only need each payment's records in order), and let the payout job group by shop when it adds up the totals. Keep this check as a test, and run it again when the traffic changes.

lab.title: Write the key-to-partition rule and prove it on a real producer
steps: Run the tests from the `labs` folder with the command above. Tests are small programs that check your code and say what's wrong. 13 of 15 fail for now. The two that pass need no code from you: one checks the `murmur2` you were given against Kafka's own, and one shows a real producer sending records without a key in long runs.

In `KeyPartitioner.java`, write `toPositive`, then `partitionFor`: UTF-8 bytes, `murmur2`, `toPositive`, then the remainder by the partition count. `KeyPartitionerTest` compares your answers with Kafka's own client library for 10,000 keys and six partition counts.
In `KeyOrdering.kt`, write `keysOutOfOrder`, `firstGlobalBreak` and `partitionsByKey`. `KeyOrderingTest` runs them on the six records from the stepper.
Write `movedKeys` with your `partitionFor`. The test expects about three keys in four to move from 6 to 8 partitions; its comment has the arithmetic.

Run everything. `KeysOnBrokerTest` starts a real Kafka 4.4 broker in Docker, sends 1,000 payments for 10 accounts into 6 partitions, and checks three things: the producer chose your partition for every record, each key came back in order, and the whole stream didn't. Its last test grows a topic to 8 partitions and checks that exactly the keys from your `movedKeys` ended up in two partitions.
hints: `number & 0x7fffffff` clears the top bit and keeps the other 31. `Math.abs` gives a different partition for most negative hashes, and `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` is still negative, because the positive number it would need doesn't fit in an `int`.
Hash the bytes, not the String: `key.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8)`. The test includes `"é"`, which is one character and two bytes.
In Kotlin, `groupBy({ it.key!! }, { it.partition })` maps each key to the list of its partitions, and `.mapValues { (_, ps) -> ps.toSet() }` turns each list into a set. Filter out null keys first.

drill.title: Place a key from memory
drill.prompt: Write `partitionFor(String key, int numPartitions)` from memory, in Java or Kotlin, using `Utils.murmur2`. Then work it out by hand: `acct-17` hashes to -1871546916. (a) Which partition of 6 does it get? (b) Which partition would `Math.abs` give? Compare with the answer.

recap: The producer picks the partition, inside your program, before the record leaves it. For a record with a key, it works out `(murmur2(key bytes) & 0x7fffffff) % partitions`.
The same key always lands in the same partition, so records with one key keep the order in which they reached the leader. Across partitions there is no order.

Records without a key go in sticky runs. Since Kafka 3.3 (KIP-794), the producer switches partition after between `batch.size` and twice `batch.size` bytes, leaning toward partitions with short queues.
Key payments by account id, for per-account order and an even spread. A hot key, such as a shop with 30% of the payments, overloads one partition and its one consumer.

The limit: the rule depends on the partition count. Growing a topic from 6 to 8 partitions moves about three keys in four while their old records stay behind, so choose the count up front, or drain before you grow.
Other client libraries may hash differently: librdkafka uses CRC32 by default and needs `partitioner=murmur2_random` to match Java.
closing:
We started with a refund that showed up before its payment. One key per account puts both in the same partition, and inside a partition, order holds. Across partitions nothing does, and a topic that grows quietly moves most of its keys.

Look at an app that shows you a list of your own events, such as your bank's payments or a chat. When two items arrive while you're offline, does their order ever surprise you? Ask what the app might be using as its key.

Next, we'll follow a record after `send()`: how it waits in a batch, what the broker answers, and how a retry can write one payment twice.

quiz.q: A Go program built on librdkafka, with default settings, and a Java program both write to `payments`, with the account id as the key. What happens?
options: Nothing goes wrong: the broker hashes the key, so every client agrees
One account can end up in two partitions, because librdkafka hashes with CRC32 by default; set `partitioner=murmur2_random` in the Go program
The broker rejects records whose key hash doesn't match the Java rule
Only records with no key differ between the two
quiz.why: The partition is picked in each client library, so two libraries with different hash functions disagree about records with keys. librdkafka's default, `consistent_random`, uses CRC32; `murmur2_random` matches the Java producer. The first option is the common belief. It fails because the broker never sees a hash: each record arrives already addressed to a partition.

quiz.q: `settlements`, the topic that feeds the nightly payouts to shops, has 12 partitions and 12 consumers in one group, and it's keyed by shop id. One shop brings 40% of all payments. What do you see?
options: An even load: murmur2 spreads keys evenly
The broker splits the shop's records over several partitions once one gets busy
One consumer handles at least 40% of all records and falls behind while the others sit idle, and adding consumers doesn't help
The producer moves the shop's records to less busy partitions (adaptive partitioning)
quiz.why: Every record with that key goes to one partition, and one consumer per group reads it. murmur2 spreads different keys evenly, but it can't split one key. Adaptive partitioning only steers records without a key; a record with a key always goes to its hash partition.

quiz.q: A producer sends 100-byte records with no key, as fast as it can, with `batch.size=16384`. How are they spread over 6 partitions?
options: In runs: a few hundred records (16 to 32 KB) to one partition, then a switch to another, favouring partitions with short queues
One record to each partition in turn, round robin
All to partition 0 until it is full
By a hash of the record's value
quiz.why: Since Kafka 3.3, the producer sticks to one partition until it has sent between `batch.size` and twice `batch.size` bytes there, then picks another at random, leaning away from long queues. Round robin was the rule before Kafka 2.4. Partitions are never "full", and the value is never hashed.

quiz.q: From Partitions and segments on disk: `payments`, keyed by account, grows from 6 to 8 partitions while its consumers are a minute behind. Which can happen?
options: Nothing changes for existing accounts: a key keeps its partition once it has one
Kafka moves the old records of each account to its new partition
The topic is unavailable until every consumer has caught up
An account's new records land in a different partition and are handled before its older, still unread records
quiz.why: The partition is worked out again for every record, from the hash and the new count; nothing remembers an old choice. About three keys in four move, while their old records stay where they were, in a partition whose consumer is still behind. Kafka never moves records between partitions: Partitions and segments on disk showed that each partition is a separate log, and partitions can be added but never merged or removed.

quiz.q: You send `ProducerRecord("payments", 3, "acct-17", value)`, which names partition 3, to a 6-partition topic. `acct-17` hashes to partition 2. Where does the record go?
options: Partition 2: the key always wins
Partition 3: an explicit partition skips the partitioner, and the key is still stored with the record
Both partitions, one copy each
The send fails because the key and the partition disagree
quiz.why: The producer checks for a partition number first, and only calls the partitioner when there is none. The key is still written with the record, so consumers see it, and so does compaction (keeping the last record per key, from Partitions and segments on disk). Mixing explicit partitions with hashed keys on one topic splits a key over two partitions, so do it only on purpose.

Why `& 0x7fffffff` and not `Math.abs` for the hash?
flashcards.back: The producer clears the sign bit. `Math.abs` gives a different partition for most negative hashes, and `Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)` is still negative.
Order within a partition: records with the same key keep the order in which they reached the leader. There is no order across partitions.

flashcards.front: Where do records with no key go, since Kafka 3.3?
flashcards.back: In sticky runs: one partition until between `batch.size` and twice that many bytes, then another, picked at random and leaning away from long queues (KIP-794).

flashcards.front: What happens to keys when a topic grows from 6 to 8 partitions?
flashcards.back: About three in four move to a new partition, and their older records stay in the old one, so per-key order can break.
The producer spreads records with keys like records without. The key is still stored, but per-key order is gone.

flashcards.front: Which librdkafka setting matches the Java producer's partitioning?

terms.plain: The code in the producer that picks a partition for each record.
An optional value sent with a record. The default partitioner hashes it to pick the partition; you choose what it is, such as the account id.
A function that turns any bytes into a number. The same bytes always give the same number, and similar bytes give unrelated numbers.
The fast 32-bit hash function the Java producer applies to the key's bytes.
Records with the same key land in one partition, so they're read in the order they reached the leader.
For records without a key: send a run of records to one partition, then switch, so batches fill up.
A key that carries a large share of the traffic, so its one partition, and that partition's consumer, get far more work than the rest.

explain_back.prompt: A friend says: "Kafka keeps our payment events in order." Explain exactly which order Kafka keeps, how the key fits in, and two things that would break it.
explain_back.answer: Kafka keeps order inside a partition and nowhere else. The producer hashes each record's key with murmur2 and takes the remainder by the partition count. So every event for one account, keyed by account id, lands in the same partition and is read in the order it reached the leader. Events for different accounts sit in different partitions with no order between them, which is fine, because we only need each account's history in order. Two things break it. If the key isn't the account id, or is missing, one account's events spread over several partitions, and a refund can be handled before its payment. And if someone adds partitions, most accounts hash to a new partition while their older events are still in the old one, so new events can overtake old ones. Two copies of our program racing on the same account also land in arrival order, not real-world order.

deeper.body:
The partitioner is a plug-in point. `partitioner.class` takes any class that implements `org.apache.kafka.clients.producer.Partitioner`, whose `partition(topic, key, keyBytes, value, valueBytes, cluster)` method returns a partition number; the producer rejects a negative one. Kafka ships `RoundRobinPartitioner`, but its own documentation warns that it can spread records unevenly (KAFKA-9965, an entry in Kafka's bug tracker). Write your own only when the default really can't express the rule, for example to give a few known hot shops partitions of their own. Every producer, and every program that joins two topics on the key, must then use the same class.

That last point matters for Kafka Streams, a library for programs that read topics, combine and transform records, and write new topics (Kafka Streams: tables, state and windows, in the Stream processing track). Joining two topics on a key needs them **co-partitioned**: the same number of partitions and the same key-to-partition rule, so that `acct-17` is in partition 2 of both. Streams uses the same murmur2 rule as the producer by default. That's why a topic written by a librdkafka client with default settings can't be joined correctly with one written from Java.

One more detail of the sticky rule. The producer counts the bytes it has handed to the current partition. After `batch.size` bytes, it switches only if that partition's open batch is full at that moment, so the switch lands at the end of a batch. After twice `batch.size`, it switches whatever the batch looks like. An exact fit is rare, which is why the Try it's runs were about 32 KB, the cap. KIP-794 explains the trade: a switch in the middle of a batch would leave a small batch behind on the old partition.
